title: The Exam That Broke: How a Pune Professor and an NTA Insider Unravelled India’s Biggest Medical Entrance Test
excerpt: CBI arrests reveal an organised syndicate that sold NEET-UG 2026 questions for as little as ₹2 lakh — and 22 lakh students must now sit a retest on June 21
body:
For the second time in three years, India’s single-window medical entrance examination has been cancelled after a paper leak — and this time the trail leads straight inside the body that was supposed to guard it.

On May 3, roughly 22 lakh students sat NEET-UG 2026 at centres across the country. Within hours, screenshots of question papers began circulating on social media. Within days, the Central Bureau of Investigation registered an FIR, raided premises in five states, and arrested what it calls the “kingpin” of the operation: P.V. Kulkarni, a chemistry professor based in Pune who allegedly dictated exam questions to batches of students at his residence before test day.

**A syndicate with an insider**

The CBI’s investigation has so far netted nine accused. The most damaging arrest is that of Manisha Gurunath Mandhare, a botany lecturer who held an official NTA appointment — making her one of the question-paper setters with direct access to the sealed exam. Investigators allege Mandhare extracted biology questions and funnelled them to Kulkarni’s network, which then sold access for sums ranging from ₹2 lakh to ₹25 lakh per student.

The modus operandi was grimly analogue. Kulkarni ran what he called “coaching classes” from his Pune home. Students — or their parents — paid cash. He then dictated questions and, in some cases, answers. Handwritten notes recovered during raids matched 90 biology and 45 chemistry questions on the actual exam paper, the CBI said.

Arrests have been made in Jaipur, Gurugram, Nashik, Pune, and Ahilyanagar. Middlemen who connected students to the network are still being traced, and the CBI has not ruled out further NTA insiders being involved.

**22 lakh students in limbo**

The National Testing Agency cancelled NEET-UG 2026 on May 10 and announced a retest for June 21 — the third time in four years that an NTA-conducted exam has been scrapped or rescheduled after integrity failures. The 2024 debacle, which centred on a Bihar-based syndicate, led to a Supreme Court hearing, widespread protests, and the forced resignation of the NTA’s then director-general.

This time, the fallout is already deeper. A petition before the Supreme Court demands the NTA’s abolition, arguing that its “pattern of systemic failure” renders it unfit to conduct high-stakes examinations. The petitioners cite the 2024 Bihar leak, the 2025 CUET glitches, and now the 2026 NEET breach as evidence of structural rot.

Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has responded by appointing fresh joint secretaries and directors to the NTA and announcing that NEET will shift to a computer-based test format from 2027. A seven-member reform committee has recommended digital question-paper delivery, biometric verification at centres, and real-time AI proctoring. But those measures arrive a year too late for the current cohort.

**The diaspora dimension**

The scandal carries particular weight for the Indian diaspora. NEET is the sole gateway to undergraduate medical seats in India, and a significant number of aspirants each year are NRI, OCI, or PIO candidates — students born and raised abroad whose parents want them trained in India’s medical system, or who see an Indian MBBS as a cost-effective route to a global medical career.

For these families, the leak is not merely an administrative failure. It is a betrayal of the compact that a centralised, transparent examination is fairer than the regional patronage networks it replaced. If NEET itself can be bought, the argument for sitting it from Houston, Dubai, or London collapses.

**What comes next**

The CBI probe is far from over. Investigators are examining digital footprints, phone records, and banking transactions to map the full network. The Supreme Court is expected to hear the NTA-abolition petition before the June 21 retest. And the political blame game — Congress has alleged BJP-linked operatives facilitated the leak in Rajasthan — will intensify as state elections approach.

Meanwhile, a 21-year-old aspirant in Uttar Pradesh allegedly died by suicide after the cancellation, a grim reminder that for millions of young Indians, NEET is not merely a test but a life-defining threshold. For 22 lakh students, the immediate reality is starker: another month of uncertainty, another round of revision, and the gnawing suspicion that the exam they worked years to prepare for may never be truly secure.
